analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant pollution nationwide, requires growing shares of renewable electricity, and funds state energy programs.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee held three days of hearings in April 2000 but never brought the bill to a vote, and it died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set nationwide yearly limits on four pollutants from large power plants — carbon dioxide, mercury, nitrogen oxide, and sulfur dioxide — with fines for exceeding them. It would have required electricity sellers to get a rising share of power from renewable sources, reaching 20% by 2020, and created a small per-kilowatt-hour charge on the grid to fund state programs for renewable energy, affordable and universal electric service, and conservation. It also would have let households with rooftop solar or other small renewable systems sell excess power back to their utility at retail rates, and forced electric companies to tell customers what fuels and pollution are behind their power.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal-fired power plants, who would see less mercury, smog, and acid-rain pollution; households that install rooftop solar or small wind, who could credit excess power against their bills; and consumers, who would get standardized fuel and emissions labels for their electricity. States would get federal matching money for energy efficiency and low-income service programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near power plants and rooftop-solar households

how_it_helps.text: Sets nationwide annual caps on carbon dioxide, mercury, nitrogen oxide, and sulfur dioxide from large combustion power plants, with per-ton civil penalties for exceeding allocations [S2][S3]
Requires a rising renewable share of electricity sold, from 2.5% in 2000 to 20% by 2020, enforced through tradeable renewable energy credits [S2][S3]

Creates a public benefits fund financed by a charge on electricity carried over the wires, matching state spending on renewable energy, universal and affordable electric service, and conservation [S2][S3]

Requires every electric company to allow customers with small renewable systems (up to 100 kilowatts) to net meter — crediting excess generation against their bill at normal retail rates with no extra standby charges [S3]
Requires utilities to disclose fuel sources and emissions to consumers, with inaccurate disclosure treated as a deceptive practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Coal-fired and other large fossil-fuel power plants, which would face nationwide emission limits, monitoring equipment costs, and penalties; some of those costs would likely reach consumers through electricity prices, and all electricity users would pay the small wires charge (capped at 0.2 cents per kilowatt-hour) that funds the state programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil-fuel power plants, and ratepayers via prices

drawbacks.text: The bill relies on tradeable emissions credits, so individual plants that buy credits could keep polluting above their allocation; it only bars a plant from exceeding 125% of the performance standard if regulators find significant local harm [S3]

The wires charge and compliance costs would flow into electricity bills, hitting households in coal-dependent regions hardest; the bill itself does not shield low-income customers from those price effects [S3]

It repeals the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act's cogeneration and small power production provisions, removing rules that had required utilities to buy power from independent cogenerators and small renewable producers, though existing contracts stay valid [S2][S3]
Net metering shifts some grid costs onto utilities and other ratepayers, and unused customer credits expire each year without compensation [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health and environmental gains — binding national limits on mercury, smog, acid-rain gases, and carbon dioxide, plus a 20% renewable standard — are large and would fall on an industry whose pollution costs were previously borne by the public. The main honest costs are higher electricity prices in fossil-heavy regions and the new wires charge, and the cap-and-trade design leaves room for local pollution hot spots. The repeal of PURPA cogeneration rules is a genuine concession to incumbent utilities tucked into an otherwise pro-renewables bill.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which held three days of hearings in April 2000, but the bill was never marked up or brought to the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. James Jeffords, a Republican from Vermont, introduced the bill on July 14, 1999 with seven original cosponsors including Sens. Lieberman, Kerry, and Kennedy [S1][S3]
Fourteen senators cosponsored the bill — 12 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S4]
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources on the day of introduction [S5]
The committee held hearings on April 11, 13, and 27, 2000, printed as S.Hrg. 106-254, pt. 2, and took no further action [S5]
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-fired utilities and other fossil generators avoided the national emission caps, monitoring costs, and penalties the bill would have imposed, and incumbent utilities kept the pre-existing rules without a federal wires charge or renewable mandate.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil-fuel power plants and incumbent utilities

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided — a Republican lead sponsor with 12 of 14 cosponsors Democratic — and the Republican-controlled committee never advanced it to a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have set hard national caps on their carbon dioxide, mercury, nitrogen oxide, and sulfur dioxide emissions, with per-ton penalties and mandatory monitoring. Their pollution is the largest industrial source of the public health harms the bill targets, so avoiding the bill kept those costs on the public.

A rising renewable portfolio standard reaching 20% by 2020 would have created a guaranteed market and tradeable credits for wind, solar, biomass, and geothermal generation. The net metering right would also open the retail market to customer-owned systems.

The bill would have imposed new obligations on utilities — a wires charge, disclosure rules, and mandatory net metering — but it also repealed PURPA's requirements that they buy power from independent cogenerators and small producers, a long-standing utility ask. Its defeat left utilities free of both the burdens and the concessions.

industries.industry: Coal mining regions and coal-dependent ratepayers
industries.note: Compliance costs would fall partly on electricity bills in regions reliant on coal generation. The bill's public benefits fund and affordability programs were intended to offset some of that, but the offset is indirect.
